newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait tanker firm expects higher charter rates.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait tanker firm expects higher charter rates.

text.p: Kuwait Oil Tanker Company, expecting a record net profit for 1996/97, said on Monday tanker charter rates could rise over the next three years.
"From this year until 2000 we expect a rise in charter rates," said Deputy Managing Director Sheikh Salman al-Sabah. "We expect the same upward trend to continue."
Sheikh Salman told Reuters U.S. environmental regulations would eventually be adopted by Europe, forcing more firms to scrap vessels to acquire double hull tankers.
"Look at the scrap market...The price per tonne has dropped to $160 from $220. This is a sign of oversupply with more ships being taken out of the market," he added.
Also growing world demand and supply of crude and refined oil products will contribute to stronger charter rates.

KOTC officials said higher rates in recent months will help the firm make a record net profit in fiscal 1996/97 of 18 million dinars ($59.6 million) compared with 8.5 million dinars the previous year.

"Actual net profit until March was 14 million dinars and for the first time in the company's history we are expecting a record 18 million dinars by the end of the (fiscal) year" to June 30, 1997, Sheikh Salman said.
KOTC, surviving two Gulf wars and a financial scandal in the past decade, carries about 20 percent of Kuwait's energy exports. Kuwait has a two million barrel per day OPEC quota.
In December KOTC ordered two 309,000-tonne crude tankers from South Korea's Hyundai Industries Co at a total cost of $160 million. They are due for delivery in mid-1998.
The state oil shipping firm operates 29 crude, product and gas carriers, runs a cooking gas (butane) filling plant and is the sole agent for all carriers lifting from Kuwait.
It handles some 105 carriers a month, earning it 700,000 dinars a year. "But the United Arab Emirates is a strong competitor," said Sheikh Salman of carriers loading supplies in neighbouring UAE.
"Our private sector suppliers (of goods) should offer us more competitive prices and cut their prices so that we can better compete with UAE ports," he added.

Sheikh Salman said some market talk of the possible privatisation of KOTC was incorrect although a plan to privatise the butane plant had been approved but was put on hold "for security reasons". KOTC has some 1,400 employees, including 850 people with shipping operations.
"KOTC is a strategic state holding and the biggest proof was the (1980-88) Iran-Iraq war when we were the only firm willing to lift from Kuwait at very high war risk (insurance) premiums," he added.

Although KOTC at the time reflagged 11 vessels in the United States to enjoy American naval protection, its carriers were often the target of Iranian attacks aimed at punishing the tiny Gulf state for supporting fellow Arab Iraq in the war.
Three KOTC product carriers still fly the U.S. flag while another two have British flags.
KOTC officials said a July 1998 deadline for shipping firms to acquire ISM maritime safety certification could result in a decrease in the number of carriers available on the market.
The Kuwaiti firm launched a programme two years ago to obtain the certification and hopes to secure it later this year.

"You are going to see ports in Europe and all over requesting this certification and some of the smaller (shipping) firms would be unable to achieve the requirements," said KOTC Manager Insurance Group Faisal Ali. "This will also contribute to higher rates and only big companies will survive."
